fr:mainmatter.html:p: The key to any nameless representation of syntax is how it indicates the variables we choose to use and thus, implicitly, those we discard. Standard de Bruijn representations delay discarding maximally till the leaves of terms where one is chosen from the variables in scope at the expense of the rest. Consequently, introducing new but unused variables requires term traversal. This paper introduces a nameless 'co-de-Bruijn' representation which makes the opposite canonical choice, delaying discarding minimally, as near as possible to the root. It is literate Agda: dependent types make it a practical joy to express and be driven by strong intrinsic invariants which ensure that scope is aggressively whittled down to just the support of each subterm, in which every remaining variable occurs somewhere. The construction is generic, delivering a universe of syntaxes with higher-order metavariables, for which the appropriate notion of substitution is hereditary. The implementation of simultaneous substitution exploits tight scope control to avoid busywork and shift terms without traversal. Surprisingly, it is also intrinsically terminating, by structural recursion alone.

This is an exercise to write about something which I've been looking at recently, and will not be edited or maintained to the level at which might be expected of a Zettelkasten entry. Instead, this will be more similar to a jekyll post but still using the linking features which I like about forester (and which is the main reason I haven't totally abandoned using forester).

The nature of the topic is extremely low-tech, and so I expect-- and I intend for-- this short exposition to be readable by anyone who has considered the particular problem of encoding syntax with binders, for example by having seen the (straight-ahead, and not necessarily well-scoped) deBruijn encoding of λ-calculus. There are plenty of places to look for such an introduction and I will not curate any pointers here (although 1001 Representations of Syntax with Binding, which is mentioned below, is one).

First of all, credit where credit's due, I appreciate that Jesper Cockx wrote the nice summary 1001 Representations of Syntax with Binding, which provides a quick but reasonably comprehensive overview of the different approaches to encoding syntax which people have came up with over the years. (I should add that one "omission"-- air quotes because it would not be until 5 years after Jesper Cockx wrote 1001 Representations of Syntax with Binding-- is Well-Scoped Locally Nameless Representation of Syntax, a variation on locally nameless, which Carlo Angiuli made known to me (and Ian Ray) after his latest search for essential papers on the topic of encoding syntax and α-equivalence.)

At the end of the blog post, the co-deBruijn (spelled "co-de Buijn" in post) encoding due to Everybody's Got To Be Somewhere, is described, although my understanding is that while Jesper Cockx's summarization is not incorrect, it's also not exactly faithful to Conor McBride's presentation-- and I don't mean because Jesper Cockx "[b]rutally stripp[ed] all the categorical concepts from the paper", but because the explicit "thinnings" are absent. (Everybody's Got To Be Somewhere calls an (order-)embedding of variable contexts/scopes a "thinning".)

(I'll also call the co-deBruijn encoding "relevant syntax", since as Jesper Cockx shows in 1001 Representations of Syntax with Binding, Everybody's Got To Be Somewhere is really about the relevancy of variables-- whether the variable is used-- regardless of whether the variables are named or indices.)

Are explicit thinnings actually essential to the co-deBruijn encoding? (An alternative formulation of the question: What is materially different, whether lost or gained, by Jesper Cockx's expulsion of explicit thinnings, as compared to Conor McBride's original presentation?) I don't really know, but I think there are two minor points to be made in support of explicit thinnings:
The explicit thinnings clarify how to compare (what I'll call) more traditional encodings of syntax with co-deBruijn. I'll try to make this vague statement more precise: Maybe it's obvious to someone else-- and likely that this question is being raised seems strange--, but I don't obviously see how a co-deBruijn encoding without explicit thinnings is supposed to play the same role as traditional syntax since traditional syntax has irrelevant variables. I suppose this just leaves a design space for how to work with syntax where all variables are relevant, but a "compatibility feature" is given already by explicit thinnings. In fact, the penultimate punchline of Everybody's Got To Be Somewhere (before considerations of general syntax) is a conversion function from the deBruijn to co-deBruijn encoding of untyped λ-calculus, and although not explicitly stated, this conversion should be an equivalence-- to be made precise below.
Conor McBride's original presentation already provides a resolution to Jesper Cockx's remark that "[he's] sure there's a more elegant way to [encode lambda abstractions which use their argument versus those which don't use their argument (ie deal with the relevancy of the variable the lambda is binding)]"-- since Conor McBride's encoding of λ-abstraction pairs the body of the λ with a thinning which marks whether the bound variable is used or not.

Since, I claim, there is a seeming discrepency between how relevant syntax is presented in 1001 Representations of Syntax with Binding and Everybody's Got To Be Somewhere, in Syntax with relevant variables › Reconstructing the narrative we reconstruct Conor McBride's presentation based on our interpretation of the text. I note however that am not particulary thinking about the more general problem of general syntax with binders, which the papers on this topic (bring your own bibliography) generally consider.

Frankly, I found Everybody's Got To Be Somewhere quite difficult to read. The names in the (almost-)agda code frequently didn't make obvious sense and there was insufficient prose to really explain the bizarre looking code (of course this is subjective). But since there is (almost-)agda code, one can use it as a reference to reconstruct what Conor McBride is describing.

To start, Jesper Cockx's summary of the core idea of relevant syntax in the paragraph starting with "Since the invention of NomPa…", is quite nice. Read it and come back. I think an abridged example rubbed from Everybody's Got To Be Somewhere is the best way to see what that summary is talking about:
K ≔ λ.λ.1
coK ≔ λ.(take🙽λ.(drop🙽var)) Above, we have the (closed) K combinator as a (straight-ahead) deBruijn λ-term, and the corresponding co-deBruijn encoding. (Since we're talking about nameless syntax in this example, I'll refer to "binding sites" and "indices" instead of "variables".) The take and drop terms are so-called "thinnings", so the body of a λ-abstraction is a pairing of a thinning which says whether or not the binding site is relevant to the body, and a λ-term in the appropriate scope, where 🙽 (\fatbslash in the stmaryrd font) is Conor McBride's (strange) name for the constructor of this pair. The var term is a pointer to a binding site.

This raises three immediate questions:
What do we mean by "scope"? As Jesper Cockx's summary tells us, in relevant syntax a term has a unique scope for which every free variable is in scope, and every variable in scope is relevant. Thus for example, if a λ-abstraction is closed (has empty scope) and is marked as having a relevant binding site, the body has singleton scope.
Which binding sites do the seemingly ambiguous thinnings take and drop refer to? Here they just refer to the unique binding site of a λ.
Which binding site does the seemingly ambiguous var point to? If you take as given that K is the corresponding deBruijn term, then var must refer to the outer binding site, but how does one read off a freestanding co-deBruijn term? The principle of relevant syntax leads us-- or rather Conor McBride-- to the logical conclusion that a pointer to a binding site must have singleton scope. Thus the var refers to the outer binding site since the inner binding site is marked irrelevant by drop and thus not in the scope of the innermost body, while the outer binding is marked relevant.

We have argued that the above co-deBruijn encoding is actually unambiguous. For some extra annotations about what is exactly taken and dropped, we can use named variables as Jesper Cockx demonstrates.
K ≔ λx.λy.x
coK ≔ λx.(take x🙽λy.(drop y🙽var x))

To be fair, the thinning in a λ-abstraction is only one bit of information since there is only one bound variable, but the idea is that this framework accomodates syntax which simultaneously binds multiple variables. Thus for (untyped) λ-calculus, where the thinning is a single bit, the encoding of λ-abstractions with explicit thinnings is equivalent to Jesper Cockx's "inelegant" encoding which has two constructors for λ-abstractions-- one where the bound variable is relevant to the body, and one where the bound variable is irrelevant to the body.
We should make precise what "thinnings" are.
